Course module · Four 75-minute sessions

How Modern Software Is Built

The architecture of websites, mobile apps, installed programs, and embedded devices, explained for business students who will be building products with Claude Code and learning Python at the same time.

Audience Business students, little technical background Format Lecture with live demos and review questions Sessions 4 × 75 minutes

How to use this document

  • Each session is designed to fit in 75 minutes. Every section carries a time budget tag such as 10 min. The budgets add up to about 70 minutes, leaving 5 minutes for the review questions and spill-over.
  • Keywords students should be able to define are highlighted like architecture. Every keyword is collected in Appendix A with a short definition and a link back to where it is introduced.
  • Review questions appear at the end of each session in a yellow box marked with a question mark. The questions and their answers are repeated in Appendix B.
  • Callouts in grey are instructor notes, analogies you can use in class, and suggested live demos. Demos are optional; each session works as a pure lecture.
  • Diagrams are drawn so that you can talk through them left to right or top to bottom. Each caption states the single point the picture is making.

Software architecture sounds like a topic for engineers, but the decisions it describes are business decisions in disguise. Whether a product can handle a spike of customers on launch day, what it costs to run every month, how quickly a new feature can ship, what happens when a server fails at 2 a.m., and how a customer's password is protected are all consequences of architecture. When you use a tool like Claude Code to build a product, you will be asked to make these decisions, or at least to approve them. This module gives you the vocabulary and the mental models to do that well.

The material is deliberately cumulative. Session 1 starts with a web page that is nothing more than a text file on your laptop. By the end of Session 4 you will be able to sketch the architecture of a company like Airbnb or Shopify, explain what "Sign in with Google" actually does behind the scenes, and describe how a phone app, a desktop program, and a smart thermostat all talk to the same servers.

Session 1 · 75 minutes

From a File on Your Laptop to a Page on the Internet

We start with the simplest possible website, a single text file opened in a browser, and follow it all the way to being served to strangers over the internet. Along the way we meet the browser, the three languages of a web page, addresses, servers, and the request-and-response conversation that every website depends on.

By the end of this session students can

  • Explain the client–server model and identify the client and server in everyday examples.
  • Describe what HTML, CSS, and JavaScript each contribute to a web page.
  • Trace what happens between typing a web address and seeing a page, including DNS and HTTP.
  • Distinguish a static website from a dynamic one and explain the limits of static sites.
  • Say where Python runs in a web application and why it does not run in the browser.

1.1 Why architecture is a business topic 5 min

When an architect designs a building, they decide where the load-bearing walls go, how people move between floors, and where the plumbing runs. Change those decisions after the concrete is poured and the cost is enormous. Software has the same property. Architecture is the set of big structural decisions about a piece of software: what its major parts are, what each part is responsible for, and how the parts talk to each other.

Three reasons a business student should care:

  • Cost. Architecture decides whether you pay a few dollars a month or tens of thousands. It decides whether adding customers adds cost linearly or barely at all.
  • Risk. Architecture decides what happens when a component fails, how a data breach could occur, and whether the product survives a viral moment or collapses under it.
  • Speed. Architecture decides how fast a team (or you with an AI coding assistant) can add features without breaking what already works.

You will not be writing the load-bearing walls yourself in this course. But you will be talking to people and tools that do, and the person who cannot follow the conversation does not get a vote.

Instructor note

A good opener is to ask the class to name a website or app that "went down" recently and speculate why. Most outages trace back to a component in this module: a database, a server that ran out of capacity, a login system, a third-party service. Return to their examples as the relevant pieces appear.

1.2 Clients, servers, and programs 10 min

Almost every piece of modern software follows one pattern: one computer asks, another computer answers. The computer that asks is the client. The computer that answers is the server. Together this is the client–server model.

Two things students often get wrong about servers:

  • A server is an ordinary computer. It has a processor, memory, and a disk exactly like a laptop. It usually has no screen or keyboard because nobody sits at it. It lives in a building full of other servers (a data center) with reliable power, cooling, and a fast internet connection. It runs 24 hours a day, waiting.
  • "Server" also names a program. A web server is a program whose only job is to listen for requests and hand back web pages. The same physical computer can run several server programs at once. In conversation, "the server" means whichever of the two is obvious from context.
Analogy

A restaurant. You (the client) sit at a table and ask the waiter for a menu. The kitchen (the server) prepares what you ask for and sends it out. You never enter the kitchen and you don't need to know how it is organized to place an order. The menu is the agreed-upon list of what you may ask for. We will reuse this restaurant repeatedly; the menu becomes the API in Session 2.

Everyday examples students already use, with the client and server identified:

ActivityClientServer
Reading news on your phoneThe browser or news app on the phoneThe newspaper's computers that hold the articles
Sending a WhatsApp messageThe WhatsApp appMeta's messaging servers, which pass the message to your friend's phone (another client)
Checking your bank balanceThe banking appThe bank's servers holding account records
Asking Claude a questionThe Claude app or Claude Code on your computerAnthropic's servers running the AI model

The client for a website is nearly always a web browser: Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge. The browser is itself just a program installed on your computer. Its job is to request pages and turn what comes back into pictures and text on the screen.

1.3 A web page is three languages 15 min

Here is a surprising fact: a web page is a plain text file. You can open it in Notepad. If you save a text file with the name index.html, type a few lines into it, and double-click it, your browser will display it as a web page. No internet connection, no server, no company involved.

The text inside that file is written in up to three languages, each with a separate job.

HTML: the content and its structure

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) says what is on the page: this is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is an image, this is a link to another page. It does this with tags, labels in angle brackets that wrap the content.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>Rosenthal's Bakery</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Rosenthal's Bakery</h1>
    <p>Fresh bread every morning since 1998.</p>
    <img src="storefront.jpg" alt="Our shop">
    <a href="menu.html">See the menu</a>
  </body>
</html>

Read it aloud and it almost explains itself: <h1> is a top-level heading, <p> is a paragraph, <img> places an image stored in a file called storefront.jpg, and <a href=...> is a link (an "anchor") to another page called menu.html. HTML alone gives you a working but ugly page: black text on white, default fonts, no layout.

CSS: how it looks

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) says what the page looks like: colors, fonts, spacing, how things are arranged, what happens on a phone screen versus a desktop monitor. A CSS rule names the thing it applies to and lists the properties to change.

h1 {
  color: #7a3e12;
  font-family: Georgia, serif;
}
p {
  font-size: 18px;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

This says: every top-level heading is a warm brown in the Georgia font; every paragraph uses 18-pixel text with comfortable line spacing. The same HTML file with a different CSS file can look like a completely different website. That separation is deliberate: content people write the HTML, design people write the CSS, and neither steps on the other.

JavaScript: what it does

JavaScript is a real programming language, the only one that browsers can run, and it makes the page do things: react when a button is clicked, check that an email address looks valid before a form is sent, show a dropdown menu, load more posts as you scroll. Without JavaScript a page is a document. With it, a page becomes an application.

const button = document.querySelector("#order-button");
button.addEventListener("click", function () {
  alert("Thanks! Your order is on its way.");
});

In words: find the element on the page whose id is order-button; when it is clicked, show a message. Students in a Python course will notice that this looks like a programming language because it is one. The syntax differs from Python (curly braces, semicolons) but the ideas are the same: variables, functions, conditions, loops.

Common confusion

JavaScript and Java are unrelated languages that share half a name for 1990s marketing reasons. Java runs on servers and in Android apps. JavaScript runs in browsers (and, since 2009, on servers too, through a program called Node.js). When people say "JS" they mean JavaScript.

The browser's act of turning those text files into pixels is called rendering. Every browser does it slightly differently, which is why the same site can look marginally different in Safari and Chrome.

1.4 The static website on your own computer 5 min

A website made only of files like the ones above, files that are written once and sent to every visitor exactly as they are, is a static website. The word "static" means the content does not change depending on who is looking or when. A brochure site for a bakery, a personal portfolio, a documentation site, and a landing page are all naturally static.

The essential point for this session: a static website needs no server at all to work on your own computer. The browser reads the files straight off your disk. This is the zero-cost, zero-infrastructure starting point from which everything else in this module is built up.

Live demo (3 minutes)
  1. Create a folder on the desktop called bakery.
  2. Ask Claude Code: "Create a one-page static website for a bakery in this folder with an index.html, a style.css, and a small script that shows a greeting when a button is clicked."
  3. Double-click index.html. Point out the address bar: it starts with file:///, meaning "a file on this machine," not https://.
  4. Change one word in the HTML in a text editor, save, and refresh the browser to show the connection between the file and the page.

Notice the limitation, though. Only you can see this page. Your friend across town cannot type anything into their browser that reaches a file on your desktop. To share it with the world, the files have to be placed on a server that is always on and reachable by address. That is the subject of the next section.

1.5 How the internet delivers a page 20 min

Suppose the bakery's files are now sitting on a server somewhere. A customer types https://www.rosenthalsbakery.com/menu.html into their browser. In the roughly half a second before the page appears, a lot happens. We take it piece by piece.

The address: anatomy of a URL

The thing you type is a URL (Uniform Resource Locator). It has parts, and each part answers a different question.

  • The domain name is the human-friendly name a business rents (typically 10 to 20 dollars a year from a registrar such as GoDaddy, Namecheap, or Cloudflare). Owning the domain is owning the brand's address on the internet.
  • The path identifies a specific page or file on that server. For a static site the path is literally a file name. For dynamic sites (Session 2) the path is more like an instruction: /orders/1234 means "show me order number 1234".
  • The query string passes extra details, like a language or a search term. When you search Google, the words you typed appear in the query string of the results URL.

Finding the server: IP addresses and DNS

Computers on the internet do not find each other by name. Every connected machine has an IP address, a number such as 142.250.72.14, and traffic is routed by number. Nobody wants to memorize numbers, so the internet has a distributed phone book called DNS (Domain Name System). When you type a domain, your browser first asks DNS "what is the IP address of www.rosenthalsbakery.com?" and gets back a number. Only then does it know where to send the request.

When a business buys a domain and then signs up with a hosting company, "pointing the domain at the host" means editing a DNS record so that the name resolves to the host's IP address. It is one of the few technical tasks a founder often does personally, and it is where the phrase "DNS changes can take up to 48 hours to propagate" comes from: the phone book is copied to thousands of servers worldwide and they refresh on a schedule.

The conversation: HTTP requests and responses

Now the browser knows the number. It opens a connection to that server and speaks a language called HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol). A protocol is simply an agreed set of rules for how two computers exchange messages, the way a business letter has a conventional layout. HTTP is refreshingly readable. The browser's request looks like this:

GET /menu.html HTTP/1.1
Host: www.rosenthalsbakery.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh) Chrome/128.0
Accept-Language: en-US

Read it as: "GET me the thing at /menu.html. I'm looking for the site called www.rosenthalsbakery.com. I'm Chrome on a Mac, and I prefer English." The server's response is equally readable:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 5120

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html> ... the actual page ...

The first line carries a status code, a three-digit summary of how things went. A handful are worth knowing because they show up in everyday life:

CodeMeaningWhen you see it
200 OKSuccess, here is what you asked forEvery normal page load
301 Moved PermanentlyThat moved; go here insteadOld links that still work after a redesign
401 Unauthorized / 403 ForbiddenYou need to log in / you're not allowedTrying to open someone else's account page
404 Not FoundNo such pageA typo in the address, a deleted page
500 Internal Server ErrorThe server's own code crashedA bug in the site; the visitor did nothing wrong
503 Service UnavailableThe server is overloaded or down for maintenanceTicket sales opening, launch-day traffic

One page usually triggers many requests. The HTML arrives first; as the browser reads it, it discovers it also needs style.css, app.js, and storefront.jpg, and sends a separate request for each. A typical commercial home page today makes 50 to 150 requests. This is why "the number of requests" is a real performance metric and why the CDN in Session 3 matters.

HTTPS: the padlock

Plain HTTP sends everything as readable text, so anyone on the same coffee-shop Wi-Fi could read the pages you request and anything you type into them. HTTPS wraps the same conversation in encryption, so that only the browser and the server can read it. The padlock in the address bar means HTTPS is on. The server proves its identity with a certificate issued by a trusted authority; since 2015 these are free (from a non-profit called Let's Encrypt) and every serious hosting service turns them on automatically. There is no longer a business reason to run a site without HTTPS, and browsers actively warn visitors away from sites that do.

Getting the files onto a server: hosting

Hosting means renting space on someone else's always-on server and putting your files there. For a static website this is astonishingly cheap or free. Services such as GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel, and Cloudflare Pages will take a folder of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and serve it to the whole world, including HTTPS and a domain of your choosing, for nothing or a few dollars a month. The workflow is: put the files in the service, point your domain's DNS at it, done.

Why is it so cheap? Because serving static files is the easiest job a computer can do. The server reads a file from disk and sends it. No thinking, no computation per visitor, nothing to remember. That simplicity is the reason static sites are fast, hard to hack, and almost impossible to overload. It is also the reason they are limited, which brings us to the next section.

Instructor note

If time allows, open the browser's developer tools (F12 or right-click, Inspect) on any real site and show the Network tab. Students can watch the list of requests grow, see the status codes, and see the HTML arrive first. This makes the diagram above concrete in about 90 seconds.

1.6 Front end, back end, and the limits of static sites 10 min

Two words you will hear in every conversation about software: front end and back end. The front end is everything that runs on the user's device and that they can see and touch: the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript we have been discussing. The back end is everything that runs on the server, out of sight: the code that decides what to send, checks who you are, records your order, charges your card.

A static website is front end only. That is precisely why it is cheap, and precisely why it cannot do certain things:

  • It cannot remember anything. If a visitor fills in a form, there is nowhere for the data to go. The server just hands out files; it does not accept and store information.
  • It cannot personalise. Every visitor gets the same menu.html. There is no "Welcome back, Dana" and no shopping cart that survives a page reload, because nothing on the server knows who Dana is.
  • It cannot keep secrets. Everything in a static site is sent to the visitor's browser, so anything in it can be read by anyone. A password, a payment key, or a private price list cannot live in front-end code. This is one of the most important security rules in this module and it will return in Session 4.
  • It cannot do work on your behalf. Sending a confirmation email, charging a credit card, or generating a PDF invoice all require a program running somewhere that is not the visitor's browser.

Every one of those needs is met by adding a back end: a program on the server that receives requests, runs logic, reads and writes stored data, and produces a response tailored to the visitor. A website with a back end is a dynamic website: its pages are generated at the moment they are requested, so they can be different for every person and every moment.

Most real products mix the two. The marketing pages of a company are static; the product behind the login button is dynamic. Knowing which parts of your product genuinely need a back end, and which can be static, is one of the first cost-saving architecture decisions a founder can make.

1.7 Where Python fits 5 min

You are learning Python in parallel with this course, so it is worth saying exactly where it fits into the picture. The browser can run only JavaScript. Python does not run in the browser. Python runs on your computer when you run a script, and it runs on servers as back-end code. When a Python program on a server answers web requests, it is the "Program" box in the diagram above.

Python is one of the most popular back-end languages in the world, used at Instagram, Spotify, Netflix, Dropbox, and nearly every AI company. In Session 2 you will see a complete, working Python web server in about ten lines. The Python skills from your other course are directly the skills of writing back ends.

LanguageWhere it runsJob
HTML, CSSBrowserContent and appearance of pages
JavaScriptBrowser (also servers via Node.js)Interactivity in the page; also a common back-end language
PythonServers and your own computerBack-end logic, data processing, AI, scripts and automation
SQLDatabase serverAsking questions of stored data (Session 2)
Swift, KotlinPhonesNative iPhone and Android apps (Session 4)

A final piece of vocabulary. A developer who works on the front end is a front-end developer; one who works on the back end is a back-end developer; one who does both is a full-stack developer. "The stack" is the list of technologies a product uses, top to bottom: the front-end framework, the back-end language, the database, the hosting. When someone asks "what's your stack?", they are asking about your architecture.

Review questions

Session 1: From a file to a page on the internet

  1. In the client–server model, which side starts every conversation, and why does that matter for how servers are designed?
  2. A web page is written in up to three languages. Name each one and state in one phrase what it is responsible for.
  3. Why can you open a static website from a folder on your desktop with no internet connection, but your friend across town cannot see it?
  4. Break the URL https://shop.example.com/products/42?color=blue into its parts and say what each part tells the browser.
  5. What does DNS do, and what everyday object is it usually compared to?
  6. A customer reports seeing "500 Internal Server Error" while another reports "404 Not Found." Which one suggests a bug in your own code, and which suggests a bad link or typo?
  7. Give two things a purely static website cannot do, and explain in one sentence what has to be added to do them.
  8. Your Python course teaches you to write programs. In a web application, where would that Python code run, and why not in the visitor's browser?

Answers are in Appendix B, Session 1.

Session 2 · 75 minutes

Dynamic Websites, APIs, and Databases

Session 1 ended with a program running on the server. This session opens that box. We see what a back end actually looks like, how the front end talks to it through an API, why almost every product needs a database, and what SQL is, illustrated with a bakery that finally takes orders.

By the end of this session students can

  • Read a ten-line Python web server and say what each route does.
  • Explain what an API is, what JSON looks like, and what GET and POST mean.

2.1 Inside the back end: a Python web server 12 min

Here is a complete dynamic web server written in Python, using a popular library called Flask. It is short enough to read in full.

from flask import Flask
from datetime import datetime

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/")
def home():
    return "<h1>Rosenthal's Bakery</h1><p>Fresh bread every morning.</p>"

@app.route("/hours")
def hours():
    now = datetime.now()
    if 7 <= now.hour < 18:
        return "<p>We are <b>open</b> right now!</p>"
    return "<p>We are closed. Back at 7 a.m.</p>"

app.run(port=5000)

Walk through it slowly with the class:

  • app = Flask(__name__) creates the web server program. Flask is a framework: a bundle of pre-written code that handles the routine parts of being a web server, so the developer only writes the parts unique to the bakery. Flask, Django, and FastAPI are Python frameworks; Express and Next.js are JavaScript ones; Rails is Ruby; Spring is Java. When Claude Code builds you a web app, it will pick one of these.
  • Each @app.route("...") line is a route: it connects a path (the part of the URL after the domain) to a Python function. When a request for /hours arrives, the hours() function runs and whatever it returns is sent back as the response.
  • The hours() function is where "dynamic" happens. It checks the current time and returns different HTML depending on the answer. Two visitors a minute apart at 5:59 p.m. and 6:00 p.m. see different pages. No static file could do that.
  • app.run(port=5000) starts listening. A port is a numbered door on a computer. One machine can run many server programs, each behind a different door. Websites use port 443 (HTTPS) and 80 (HTTP) by convention, so you never type them; developers testing on their own machine use doors like 5000 or 3000, which is why you will see addresses like http://localhost:5000.

localhost means "this computer." When you run the program above and open http://localhost:5000/hours, your browser is the client, your own laptop is the server, and the request never leaves the machine. Every developer works this way before putting anything on the internet. Session 3 covers the jump from localhost to the world.

Live demo (4 minutes)
  1. Ask Claude Code to create the Flask app above and run it.
  2. Open http://localhost:5000 and http://localhost:5000/hours in a browser.
  3. Change the closing hour in the code, save, refresh. Point out that the HTML did not exist as a file anywhere; the program composed it on demand.
  4. Try http://localhost:5000/nothing to get a live 404.

In practice, back ends do not build HTML by gluing strings together. They use templates: HTML files with blanks in them, such as Welcome back, {{ customer_name }}, which the program fills in for each request. Designers can edit the template without touching the Python, and the Python can change without touching the design. The idea to carry away is the same either way: the server runs code, and the code produces the page.

2.2 APIs and JSON: how programs talk to programs 15 min

The Flask example returned HTML for a human to read. But increasingly the thing making the request is not a human's browser rendering a page. It is another program: JavaScript in the page asking for "just the data," a mobile app, a partner's system, or an AI assistant. For those callers, the server returns raw data instead of a designed page. The set of requests a server understands, and the shape of the answers it gives, is its API (Application Programming Interface).

Analogy

Back to the restaurant. The menu is the API. It lists exactly what you may order and what you will get. You do not need to see the kitchen, and the kitchen can be reorganised without changing the menu. A menu written in a standard format lets anyone order, including delivery apps that were never imagined when the restaurant opened.

A web API is reached over HTTP just like a page, but its endpoints (individual addresses) return data rather than HTML. Here is the bakery adding one:

@app.route("/api/products")
def list_products():
    return {
        "products": [
            {"id": 1, "name": "Sourdough loaf", "price": 7.50, "in_stock": True},
            {"id": 2, "name": "Rye bread",      "price": 6.00, "in_stock": False},
            {"id": 3, "name": "Challah",        "price": 8.00, "in_stock": True}
        ]
    }

A request to /api/products gets back this:

{
  "products": [
    {"id": 1, "name": "Sourdough loaf", "price": 7.5, "in_stock": true},
    {"id": 2, "name": "Rye bread", "price": 6.0, "in_stock": false},
    {"id": 3, "name": "Challah", "price": 8.0, "in_stock": true}
  ]
}

This format is JSON (JavaScript Object Notation, pronounced "Jason"). Curly braces hold a set of named values; square brackets hold a list; text is in quotes; numbers and true/false stand alone. Python students will recognise it: a JSON object is almost exactly a Python dictionary, and a JSON array is a Python list. Every programming language can read and write JSON, which is why it became the common tongue of the web.

Verbs: GET, POST, and friends

HTTP requests carry a method, a verb stating the kind of action. Static sites only ever needed GET ("give me this"). APIs use the full set:

MethodMeaningBakery exampleBusiness action
GETRead; fetch somethingGET /api/productsShow the catalogue
POSTCreate; submit new dataPOST /api/orders with the order in the bodyPlace an order
PUT / PATCHUpdate something existingPATCH /api/orders/88 with {"status": "ready"}Mark an order ready
DELETERemoveDELETE /api/orders/88Cancel an order

An API organised this way, where every URL names a thing (a product, an order) and the method says what to do to it, is called REST (or "RESTful"). Almost every API you will encounter, from Stripe to Shopify to the Claude API, is roughly REST. The letters stand for something (Representational State Transfer) that nobody needs to remember; the idea is nouns in the URL, verbs in the method.

The four verbs map to the four things any system does with data, remembered by the acronym CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete. A surprising fraction of all business software is CRUD screens over a database: customers, invoices, tickets, inventory. Recognising a product as "mostly CRUD" is a useful signal that it is well understood and inexpensive to build.

Who calls APIs?

The right-hand side of this picture is where much of modern product-building happens. A third-party API lets you rent a capability instead of building it: charge a card with Stripe, send a text message with Twilio, look up an address with Google Maps, or generate text with the Claude API. Each is usually billed per use, which turns what used to be an engineering project into a line item. Much of "using AI to build products" is, architecturally, calling the right third-party APIs from your back end.

Instructor note

Students will meet the phrase "API key" constantly. It is a long secret string a third party gives you that identifies your account when your back end calls their API, so they know whom to bill. It lives on your server, never in front-end code. We return to this in Session 4, but planting it here pays off.

2.3 Why every product needs a database 10 min

The /api/products example had its data typed directly into the program. That breaks the moment a real business touches it: the baker cannot edit Python to change a price, and an order placed by a customer has nowhere to be saved. The server needs somewhere to store data that survives restarts, can be changed by the program, and can be searched. That somewhere is a database.

Why not just save to a file, the way you might save a spreadsheet? Because a database solves problems a file cannot:

  • Many writers at once. Two customers buying the last challah at the same instant must not both succeed. A database handles this; a file being edited by two programs simultaneously gets corrupted.
  • Speed at scale. Finding one order among ten million by scanning a file takes minutes. A database with an index (like the index in a textbook) does it in milliseconds.
  • Reliability. If the power fails halfway through saving an order, a database guarantees the order is either fully saved or not saved at all, never half. This property is called a transaction. Moving money between two bank accounts is the classic case: the debit and the credit must both happen or neither.
  • Questions. "Which customers ordered rye more than three times last quarter?" is one line in a database language and a small programming project against a pile of files.

The database is a separate program, a database management system (DBMS). Your Python back end does not store data itself; it sends instructions to the DBMS and gets results back, much as the browser sends requests to the web server. In Session 3 we will see that the DBMS often runs on its own machine.

The relational model: tables

The dominant way to organise business data for the last fifty years is the relational model. Data lives in tables: each table holds one kind of thing, each row is one instance of that thing, and each column is one fact about it. The bakery needs at least these:

customers
customer_idnameemailcity
1Dana Levidana@example.comBoston
2Sam Ortizsam@example.comCambridge
3Priya Nairpriya@example.comBoston
products
product_idnameprice
1Sourdough loaf7.50
2Rye bread6.00
3Challah8.00
orders
order_idcustomer_idproduct_idquantityordered_atstatus
871322026-09-21 08:14ready
882112026-09-21 08:20baking
891212026-09-22 07:55placed

Two ideas make this work:

  • Every row has a primary key, a column whose value is unique for that row and never changes: customer_id, product_id, order_id. Names are not good keys because two customers can share one and people change theirs.
  • Instead of copying Dana's name and email into every order she places, the order stores only her customer_id. A column that holds the primary key of a row in another table is a foreign key. The orders table has two: customer_id and product_id. This is what "relational" refers to: tables related through keys.

The overall design of the tables, their columns, and the keys that link them is the schema. Designing a schema is really designing the business: what things exist, what we record about them, and how they relate. Business students are often better at this than engineers, because it is a question about the domain rather than about code.

2.4 SQL by example 15 min

Relational databases are all controlled with one language, SQL (Structured Query Language, said "sequel" or "S-Q-L"). It was designed in the 1970s to be readable by business analysts, and it largely is. You are not expected to write SQL in this course; you are expected to recognise it, read simple statements, and know what it can do. Claude Code will write the SQL, but you will be reviewing what it writes and asking for the right things.

A request to a database is a query. Six examples cover most of what a business ever needs.

Reading: SELECT

SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE city = 'Boston';

"Give me the name and email of every customer whose city is Boston." SELECT picks the columns, FROM picks the table, WHERE filters the rows. Result: Dana Levi and Priya Nair. Replace the column list with * to get every column.

Counting and summing: aggregate functions

SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS how_many
FROM orders
GROUP BY status;

"For each order status, how many orders are there?" Result: one row per status (placed 1, baking 1, ready 1). SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX work the same way. Every management dashboard in the world is a stack of queries like this.

Combining tables: JOIN

SELECT customers.name, products.name, orders.quantity
FROM orders
JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id
JOIN products  ON orders.product_id  = products.product_id
WHERE orders.status = 'placed';

This is the query that makes the relational model pay off. The orders table has only ID numbers; a JOIN stitches each order to the matching customer row and product row using the keys, so the result reads like a human wants it to: "Dana Levi, Rye bread, 1." Whenever you see a report that combines information from several places, there is a JOIN behind it.

Writing: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product_id, quantity, status)
VALUES (3, 1, 2, 'placed');

UPDATE orders SET status = 'ready' WHERE order_id = 88;

DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 89;

"Add an order: customer 3, product 1, quantity 2, status placed." "Change order 88's status to ready." "Remove order 89." The database assigns the new order its order_id automatically. Notice how much rides on the WHERE clause: DELETE FROM orders; with no WHERE deletes every order in the company. This is not a hypothetical. It is a well-known category of career-defining mistakes, and the reason production databases have backups and restricted permissions (Session 3).

Creating the structure: CREATE TABLE

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id  INTEGER REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    product_id   INTEGER REFERENCES products(product_id),
    quantity     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    ordered_at   TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    status       TEXT DEFAULT 'placed'
);

This defines the table itself: each column, its data type (whole number, timestamp, text), which column is the primary key, which columns are foreign keys (REFERENCES), and which are required (NOT NULL). The database will now refuse to save an order with no quantity, or one pointing at a customer who does not exist. Those constraints are business rules enforced by the storage layer, which is far more reliable than hoping every program remembers to check.

What students should take away
  • SQL is a language of questions and instructions about tables. It reads roughly like English.
  • Reading is SELECT; writing is INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE; structure is CREATE TABLE.
  • JOIN is how information split across tables is put back together.
  • They should be able to look at a query Claude Code writes and say "this deletes every row" or "this only fetches Boston customers."

Which database? The names you will hear

ProductTypeTypical useCost model
SQLiteRelational, single filePrototypes, phone apps, small tools. Built into Python. Claude Code will often start you here.Free, no server to run
PostgreSQL ("Postgres")Relational serverThe default choice for new web products of any sizeFree software; hosted versions charged by size and usage
MySQL / MariaDBRelational serverVery common in older web products, WordPress, many hosting packagesFree software; hosted versions charged
Microsoft SQL Server, OracleRelational serverLarge enterprises, finance, legacy systemsCommercial licences, often expensive
MongoDBDocument (NoSQL)Flexible or rapidly changing data shapesFree software; hosted service (Atlas) charged
RedisKey-value, in memoryCaching, sessions, counters (Session 3)Free software; hosted charged

All the relational ones speak SQL with minor dialect differences, so the concepts transfer. For a new product in 2026, "Postgres" is the safe default and the one you will hear most.

2.5 Beyond tables: NoSQL and ORMs 8 min

NoSQL databases

Not all data fits neatly into fixed columns. A product catalogue where every product has different attributes (shoes have sizes, laptops have memory) fights the relational model. NoSQL databases relax the rules. The most common kind, a document database such as MongoDB, stores each record as a JSON-like document with whatever fields it needs:

{
  "product_id": 3,
  "name": "Challah",
  "price": 8.00,
  "tags": ["bread", "shabbat", "egg"],
  "sizes": {"small": 6.00, "large": 8.00}
}

Flexibility has a price: the database no longer enforces that every product has a price, and combining data across collections is clumsier than a JOIN. The choice between relational and NoSQL is a genuine architecture decision, but a simple rule of thumb serves most businesses: start relational. Business data (customers, orders, invoices, inventory) is naturally tabular and you will want the guarantees. Reach for NoSQL when you have a specific reason: extremely high write volume, genuinely irregular data, or a cache.

ORMs: letting Python speak to the database

Developers rarely type SQL into their programs directly. Most use an ORM (Object-Relational Mapper), a library that lets the program treat rows as ordinary Python objects and generates the SQL behind the scenes:

# Python with an ORM (SQLAlchemy):
boston = Customer.query.filter_by(city="Boston").all()

# ...which the ORM turns into SQL for you:
# SELECT * FROM customers WHERE city = 'Boston';

When Claude Code builds a back end for you, it will almost certainly use an ORM, and files called "models" describe the tables. The point for a business reader: the concepts (tables, keys, queries) are unchanged; the ORM is a convenience layer on top of them.

2.6 Putting it together: the three-tier architecture 10 min

We now have three distinct kinds of component, and the standard name for arranging them is the three-tier architecture:

  1. Presentation tier: the front end. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in the browser (or the screens of a phone app). Shows things to people and collects their input.
  2. Application tier (also called the logic tier or the back end): the server program. Receives requests, enforces business rules, decides what to do, talks to the database, and returns responses. This is where business logic lives: prices, discounts, permissions, validation, workflows.
  3. Data tier: the database. Stores and retrieves the facts.

Follow one order through all three tiers. Dana clicks "Order 2 challahs":

Three observations that will matter for the rest of the module:

  • The browser never talks to the database directly. All access goes through the back end, which checks identity and applies rules. If a browser could send SQL, anyone could run DELETE FROM orders. This is why the front end can never be trusted with secrets or with enforcing rules; anything in the browser can be changed by the person using it.
  • Each tier can be changed independently. Redesign the front end without touching the database. Swap SQLite for PostgreSQL without changing the HTML. Rewrite the back end from Python to something else while the other two tiers carry on. This independence is the whole point of tiers.
  • Each tier can be placed on different hardware. Today all three might run on one laptop. Tomorrow the database can move to its own machine and the back end can be copied onto ten. That is Session 3.
Instructor note

Ask students to name the three tiers for an app they use daily. For Uber: the app on the phone (presentation), Uber's servers matching riders and drivers and computing fares (application), and the records of trips, drivers, and payments (data). Then ask where the surge-pricing rule lives. It is in the application tier, on the server, precisely so that no one can tamper with it from the app.

Session 3 · 75 minutes

Hosting, Scaling, and the Cloud

So far everything has run on one laptop. This session moves the bakery onto the internet and then grows it, one step at a time, from a single rented server to the distributed architecture used by companies serving millions of people. Each step is motivated by a specific problem the previous step could not solve, and each step has a price tag.

By the end of this session students can

  • Explain what deployment means and name the standard environments code moves through.
  • Describe the single-server setup and its main weakness.
  • Explain why the database is moved to its own machine.
  • Describe horizontal scaling, load balancing, and why servers must be stateless.
  • Say what a cache, a CDN, and object storage each do.
  • Distinguish IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, and serverless, and know when each is a sensible choice.

3.1 From localhost to production 10 min

The bakery's back end works beautifully at http://localhost:5000. Moving it to a place where customers can reach it is called deployment. "Deploy" is one of the most frequently used verbs in a software team, and it means exactly this: take the code that works here and make it run there.

Serious teams do not deploy straight from a laptop to customers. Code passes through environments, each a full copy of the application with its own database:

EnvironmentWho uses itPurposeData
Development ("dev", "local")Each programmer, on their own computerWrite and try code freely; break thingsFake or sample data
Staging ("test", "QA")The team, testers, sometimes the clientA private replica of production to check a release before customers see itRealistic but not real (or anonymised)
Production ("prod", "live")Real customersThe actual businessReal; protected and backed up

"It works on my machine" is the oldest joke in software precisely because development and production differ: different operating system, different database size, different traffic, different secrets. Staging exists to catch those differences before a customer does. When a founder asks "can we just push it live?" the honest engineering answer is "only if you would be comfortable finding the bugs at the same moment your customers do."

Two measures describe how well a production system is doing. Uptime is the percentage of time it is reachable; each extra "nine" is dramatically more expensive to achieve. Latency is how long each request takes to answer. Much of the architecture in this session exists to push uptime up and latency down.

UptimeDowntime allowed per yearTypical of
99%About 3.7 daysA hobby site on one cheap server
99.9% ("three nines")About 8.8 hoursA small business product with sensible hosting
99.99% ("four nines")About 53 minutesPayment, banking, large SaaS. Requires redundancy at every layer
99.999% ("five nines")About 5 minutesTelecom, critical infrastructure. Very expensive

3.2 Step 1: everything on one server 10 min

The simplest deployment is to rent one computer in a data center and install everything on it. Cloud companies rent these by the hour or month as virtual private servers (VPS) from providers such as DigitalOcean, Linode, Hetzner, or Amazon's EC2, for as little as 5 dollars a month. "Virtual" because one powerful physical machine is carved into several independent virtual ones, each of which feels to its renter like a whole computer.

On that one machine you install:

  • An operating system, almost always Linux on servers. Linux is free, stable, and what nearly all server software is built for. Windows and macOS run desktops; iOS and Android run phones; Linux runs the internet.
  • The web server program (Nginx is the usual choice), which accepts connections on ports 80 and 443, handles HTTPS, serves the static files itself, and forwards dynamic requests to the back end.
  • Your back-end program (the Python/Flask app), listening on an internal port such as 5000.
  • The database (PostgreSQL), listening on its own internal port, 5432 by convention.

Do not underestimate this setup. A modest 20-dollar server can comfortably handle tens of thousands of visits a day, which covers most small businesses and every early-stage prototype. Its weaknesses only appear with growth:

  • Single point of failure. If the machine's disk dies, or the data center loses power, or you make a mistake while updating it, the website and the database disappear together. A single point of failure is the enemy of uptime.
  • Resource contention. The database and the back end compete for the same memory and processor. A heavy report query can make the website slow for every visitor.
  • Hard ceiling. When traffic outgrows the machine, the only option is a bigger machine, and machines do not get infinitely big.
  • Security blast radius. If an attacker breaks into the web server, they are already sitting on the same machine as all the customer data.

Each of the following steps removes one of these weaknesses, and each adds cost and complexity. Good architecture means taking the next step when the problem is real, not before.

3.3 Step 2: give the database its own machine 10 min

The first thing to move off the shared server is the database. It goes onto a second machine, a dedicated database server, and the back end connects to it over the network instead of talking to it on the same box.

Why this is worth the second bill:

  • Right-sized hardware. Databases want lots of memory and fast disks; web servers want processor cores and network bandwidth. Separated, each can be bought for what it actually needs.
  • Security. The database server gets a private network address only. There is no route from the internet to it. A firewall allows connections on port 5432 only from the web server. An attacker who compromises the web server still has another wall to get through, and no one can stumble across the customer records from outside.
  • Independent failure and maintenance. The web server can be rebuilt, upgraded, or replaced without touching a byte of data. Backups of the database run without slowing the website.
  • It unlocks the next step. With the data in one shared place, you can now run more than one copy of the web server, which is what Step 3 does.

In practice, almost nobody installs PostgreSQL on a rented machine themselves any more. Cloud providers offer a managed database, such as Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL, Supabase, or Neon: you click "create PostgreSQL," and they run the machine, take nightly backups, install security patches, and can switch to a standby copy automatically if the primary fails. You get a connection address and a bill, starting around 15 to 50 dollars a month. For nearly every business this is the correct choice; running your own database is expertise you do not want to have to hire.

3.4 Step 3: many web servers behind a load balancer 15 min

The bakery is featured on a national morning show. Ten thousand people open the site in the same minute. The single web server, already the busiest machine, runs out of capacity and starts answering with 503 errors. There are two ways to add capacity, and their names are worth knowing because they come up in every scaling conversation.

  • Vertical scaling ("scaling up"): replace the machine with a bigger one. Simple, no code changes. But the biggest machine money can buy is still finite, price grows faster than capacity, and there is still exactly one of it.
  • Horizontal scaling ("scaling out"): keep the machines modest but run several identical copies of the web server. Twice the traffic, twice the servers. In principle there is no ceiling; this is how every large internet company works.

The load balancer

Several web servers create an immediate question: the domain name resolves to one IP address, so which server does a customer's request go to? The answer is a new component that sits in front of all of them, the load balancer. The public address belongs to the load balancer. It accepts every request and forwards each to one of the servers behind it, spreading the work evenly (round-robin, or to whichever is least busy). It also performs health checks: every few seconds it pings each server, and if one stops answering it simply stops sending it traffic. Customers never notice.

The catch: servers must be stateless

Horizontal scaling has one requirement that shapes how back ends are written. Consider a customer who logs in. Their first request goes to web server 1, which notes "this person is Dana, logged in." Their next click is routed by the load balancer to web server 2, which has never heard of them and asks them to log in again. The site appears broken.

The solution is that web servers must be stateless: they remember nothing between requests. Everything that needs remembering (who is logged in, what is in the shopping cart) is stored somewhere all the servers can reach: the database, or a fast shared store such as Redis. Any server can then handle any request, because the information travels with the request (in a cookie, as Session 4 explains) and the facts live in the shared store. Statelessness is what makes servers interchangeable, and interchangeable servers are what make it possible to add ten more during the morning show and remove them after lunch.

This step is also the one that turns "the server is down" from a disaster into a non-event. With two or more servers behind a load balancer, one can fail, be updated, or be replaced while the others carry on. Redundancy at every layer, including the database, is what the industry calls high availability, and it is how three and four nines of uptime are bought.

Business translation

Horizontal scaling is what makes cloud costs elastic: pay for eight servers during Black Friday and two in February. It is also why a founder should ask, before launch, "Can we run two copies of this?" If the answer is no, because the code keeps things in memory on one machine, the first traffic spike will expose it.

3.5 Step 4: caches, CDNs, and storage 10 min

With the servers scaled, the next bottlenecks are usually the database and the distance between servers and customers. Three components address them.

Cache

A cache is a fast, temporary copy of something that was expensive to produce. The bakery's product list is requested thousands of times a minute and changes twice a day. Running the same SQL query thousands of times is wasteful; the back end runs it once, keeps the result in memory (typically in Redis, the same in-memory store used for sessions), and hands out the copy for the next 60 seconds. Database load drops by a thousand-fold. Caches appear everywhere: your browser caches images so it does not re-download them, servers cache query results, and the CDN below is a cache too. Their one hard problem is staleness: the copy can be out of date, so someone must decide how long a copy may live and when to throw it away.

Content delivery network

A customer in Singapore requesting an image from a server in Virginia waits for the bytes to cross the Pacific twice, about 200 milliseconds, before anything appears. A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a company with servers in hundreds of cities that keeps copies of your static files (images, CSS, JavaScript, video) near your users. The Singaporean customer gets the image from Singapore in 10 milliseconds, and your own servers never see the request at all. Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, and Amazon CloudFront are the household names. Most of the bytes of most websites are served by a CDN, not by the site's own servers, and CDNs also absorb the flood of junk traffic in a denial-of-service attack.

Object storage

Customers upload photos; the bakery publishes menus as PDFs; the app records videos. Files like these should not live on a web server's disk, because with three web servers a file uploaded to server 1 is invisible to servers 2 and 3. They go into object storage, a cloud service designed to hold unlimited files at fractions of a cent per gigabyte and hand them out by URL. Amazon S3 is the original and the name people use generically; Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and Cloudflare R2 are equivalents. The database stores the address of the photo; the photo itself is in object storage, usually behind the CDN.

Read replicas

Finally, the database itself can be partially scaled. Most applications read far more than they write. A read replica is a continuously updated copy of the primary database that answers read-only queries (product lists, order history, reports) while all writes still go to the one primary. A replica also serves as a hot spare: if the primary fails, the replica is promoted and the site carries on. Splitting writes across several databases (called sharding) is the hard, expensive step that only very large companies take; it is beyond this course, but you should know the word.

This picture, or something very like it, is what runs behind most products you use. Naming its parts and explaining why each exists is the core competence this module aims for. Notice that nothing conceptually new was added after Session 2: it is still presentation, application, and data. Everything in this session was about copies, placement, and failure.

3.6 The cloud menu: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, serverless 10 min

Everything above can be rented rather than owned, and cloud computing is simply the name for that arrangement: someone else owns the data centers and you pay for what you use. Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud are the giants; there are many smaller, simpler providers. The real decision is not which brand but how much of the work you want to do yourself, and the industry describes that choice in layers.

LayerYou getYou manageExamplesGood for
IaaS
Infrastructure as a Service		Virtual machines, disks, networksOperating system, web server, database, security patches, scaling, backupsAmazon EC2, Google Compute Engine, DigitalOcean, HetznerTeams with operations expertise; unusual requirements
PaaS
Platform as a Service		"Here is my code; run it"Just your code and your dataHeroku, Render, Railway, Fly.io, Vercel, Netlify, Google App EngineStartups, small teams, anything built with Claude Code
SaaS
Software as a Service		A finished productYour account settingsGmail, Salesforce, Shopify, Slack, Notion, QuickBooksEverything you do not need to build yourself
Serverless
(Functions as a Service)		Run this function when something happensJust the function's codeAWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Functions, Google Cloud FunctionsSpiky or infrequent workloads; glue between services
Analogy

Getting a pizza. IaaS is renting a kitchen: you bring ingredients and cook. PaaS is a meal kit: ingredients and instructions arrive, you assemble. SaaS is delivery: a finished pizza at the door. Serverless is a vending machine that bakes a slice when you press the button and charges you only for that slice. Each step to the right costs more per unit but less in effort and staff, and the right answer depends on how many pizzas you sell and whether pizza is your business.

Two more terms fill out the vocabulary. A container (made with a tool called Docker) packages a program with everything it needs so it runs identically on a developer's laptop and on any cloud, which largely cures "it works on my machine." Kubernetes is the system that runs and scales thousands of containers across many machines; it is powerful, complex, and almost never the right first choice for a small team. When people say "we containerised the app," they mean it is now portable across all the layers above.

For students in this course, the practical guidance is direct. A prototype built with Claude Code is best deployed on a PaaS (Render, Railway, Vercel, Fly.io) with a managed database (Supabase, Neon, or the PaaS's own). That gives you Steps 1 through 3 of this session, including HTTPS, load balancing, and horizontal scaling, for somewhere between 0 and 50 dollars a month, without ever logging into a server. Move down to IaaS only when you have a specific reason and someone to operate it.

3.7 Shipping code safely 5 min

Three practices make it possible to change a live product without breaking it, and you will see all three in any team you work with.

  • Version control. Every change to the code is recorded, with author and reason, and can be undone. The tool is Git; GitHub and GitLab host the shared copies. A repository ("repo") is one project's history. Claude Code works inside Git repositories and can commit changes for you; knowing that the history exists, and that anything can be rolled back, is what makes experimenting safe.
  • CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment). Automation that runs the tests every time code changes and, if they pass, deploys it. Instead of a risky quarterly release, teams ship small changes many times a day. On a PaaS this is often built in: connect your GitHub repo, and every change to the main branch goes live within minutes.
  • Monitoring and logging. Servers write a line to a log for every request and every error; monitoring tools (Datadog, Sentry, Grafana) collect them, chart them, and page someone at 2 a.m. if the error rate jumps. A product without monitoring finds out about outages from angry customers.

Identity, Security, and Software Beyond the Browser

Every architecture so far has quietly assumed the server knows who is asking. This session explains how it finds out: passwords, cookies and sessions, Basic Auth, and OAuth, the mechanism behind every "Sign in with Google" button. We then widen the lens from websites to phone apps, installed programs, and embedded devices, and finish with where AI services fit in the picture.

By the end of this session students can

  • Distinguish authentication from authorization with examples.
  • Explain why passwords are hashed and what multi-factor authentication adds.
  • Describe how a cookie keeps a user logged in across stateless requests.
  • Explain HTTP Basic Authentication and why it is only acceptable over HTTPS.
  • Walk through the OAuth authorization-code flow and explain what it protects.
