4.1 Authentication versus authorization 8 min

Two words that sound alike and are constantly confused, even by professionals. Keep them apart with two questions.

  • Authentication answers "Who are you?" It is the act of proving identity: a password, a code from your phone, a fingerprint, or a login through Google. Shortened to "authn" or just "auth".
  • Authorization answers "What are you allowed to do?" Once the system knows you are Dana, may Dana see order 90? May Dana see Sam's order 88? May Dana issue a refund? Shortened to "authz".
Analogy

An office building. Showing your badge at the front desk is authentication: they confirm you are an employee. Which doors your badge opens is authorization: the server room is not among them unless you are in IT. A guest badge authenticates you as a visitor and authorizes almost nothing.

Authorization is usually organised through roles: customer, staff, manager, administrator. Rules are written per role ("staff may mark orders ready; only managers may refund") and users are assigned roles. Deciding the roles and rules of a product is a business question, not a technical one, and it is one you should expect to answer when you build something.

A rule of thumb that catches most authorization bugs in the wild: every request that touches a specific record must check that this user may touch this record. Systems that check "is the user logged in?" but forget "is this their order?" allow anyone to read anyone's data by changing the number in the URL. This exact flaw has produced many of the largest data leaks of the last decade.

4.2 Passwords done right 8 min

The oldest authentication method is a shared secret: the user and the server both know the password. The obvious design, storing each user's password in the database next to their email, is also the most dangerous thing a product can do. If the database is ever stolen (and databases are stolen constantly), every password is exposed, and since people reuse passwords, so are their bank and email accounts.

The correct design stores a hash of the password instead. A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length scramble in a way that cannot be reversed. correct-horse-battery might hash to $2b$12$K9xT…. To check a login, the server hashes what the user typed and compares the two scrambles. The server never needs the original password, and a thief who steals the database gets scrambles they cannot turn back into passwords. (Details you may hear: passwords are "salted," meaning a random value is mixed in so identical passwords do not produce identical hashes, and slow algorithms such as bcrypt or argon2 are used so that guessing billions of passwords takes years.)

The lesson for a product owner is simple and non-negotiable: if a system can email you your old password, it is storing passwords wrongly. A correctly built system can only reset a password, never reveal it.

Passwords alone are weak because people choose bad ones and reuse them. Multi-factor authentication (MFA, or two-factor, 2FA) adds a second, independent proof: something you have (a code from an authenticator app or a hardware key) or something you are (a fingerprint or face) on top of something you know (the password). A stolen password alone then no longer opens the account. Every serious product should offer it, and every business should require it for staff accounts. Newer passkeys go further and replace passwords with a cryptographic key stored on your device, unlocked by fingerprint or face; they are becoming the default on major platforms.

4.3 Staying logged in: cookies, sessions, and tokens 10 min

Session 3 established that HTTP is stateless: each request arrives with no memory of the last. Yet you log in once and stay logged in for weeks. How does the server recognise you on the second request?

The mechanism is the cookie. When you log in successfully, the server's response includes an instruction: "browser, please store this piece of text and send it back to me with every future request." The browser obeys automatically. The text is usually a session ID: a long random string that means nothing by itself but which the server has recorded in its session store (the Redis box in Session 3) alongside "this is Dana, logged in at 8:14, expires in 14 days." Each request carries the cookie; the server looks up the ID; now it knows who is asking. Log out, and the server deletes the record so the ID becomes worthless.

Three consequences worth drawing out:

  • The cookie is as good as the password while it lasts. Anyone who copies the session cookie can act as Dana until it expires. This is why cookies are marked to be sent only over HTTPS and never be readable by JavaScript, and why sensitive actions (changing the password, paying) often ask for the password again.
  • This is how any web server in a load-balanced pool can serve Dana. The identity travels with the request; the facts live in the shared store. Stateless servers, from Session 3, depend on exactly this.
  • Cookies are also how advertising tracks people. The same mechanism that remembers your login lets a third-party advertising server recognise your browser across every site that shows its ads. Cookie-consent banners and privacy laws exist because of that second use, not the first.

Mobile apps and APIs often use a variant: instead of a random ID that the server looks up, the server issues a token: a signed piece of text that itself says "Dana, valid until Friday" and cannot be forged because it carries a signature only the server could produce. The most common format is the JSON Web Token (JWT, said "jot"). The client sends the token in an Authorization header rather than a cookie. The concept is identical: prove who you are once, receive a credential, present the credential thereafter.

4.4 HTTP Basic Authentication and API keys 7 min

Before cookies and tokens there was the simplest possible scheme, built into HTTP itself and still in use: HTTP Basic Authentication. When a server requires it, the browser pops up its own plain grey username/password box (you have probably seen one on a router or a staging site). The browser then attaches the credentials to every request:

GET /admin/reports HTTP/1.1
Host: www.rosenthalsbakery.com
Authorization: Basic ZGFuYTpjb3JyZWN0LWhvcnNl

That jumble after Basic is not encryption. It is Base64 encoding of the text dana:correct-horse, and anyone can decode it in a second. Basic Auth therefore has two rules and two uses:

Rules

  • Only ever over HTTPS. Over plain HTTP the password crosses the network in the clear on every request.
  • Only for things where a shared, static password is acceptable. There is no logout, no expiry, no second factor.

Where you still meet it

  • Putting a quick password in front of a staging site so the public cannot see it.
  • Internal tools and admin pages for a handful of staff.
  • Some APIs, where the "username" is an account ID and the "password" is a key. Stripe's API, for instance, accepts your secret key this way.

A close cousin is the API key, which we met in Session 2. It is a long random secret issued by a service provider that your back end presents with each call so the provider knows whose account to bill and what it may do. Keys are passwords for programs, and they must be treated as such: stored in server configuration (a file called .env is the convention), never typed into front-end code, and never committed into a Git repository. Automated bots scan GitHub around the clock for accidentally published keys and can spend thousands of dollars of someone's cloud budget within minutes. When you use Claude Code with the Claude API or any other service, this is the single most important habit to build.

4.5 OAuth: how "Sign in with Google" works 15 min

Two problems appear the moment products start working together. First, a new app wants to let users sign up without inventing yet another password, so it offers "Sign in with Google" or "Continue with Apple." Second, an app wants to use another service on the user's behalf: a scheduling tool that reads your Google Calendar, an accounting app that pulls transactions from your bank, a Claude integration that reads your Notion pages. The naive solution to both, asking the user to type their Google password into the new app, is catastrophic: the app would then hold a password that opens everything, forever, and the user could revoke it only by changing the password everywhere.

OAuth 2.0 solves both problems with one idea: the user never gives the app their password. Instead, the user is sent to the service they already trust (Google), approves a specific, limited request there, and the trusted service hands the app a special-purpose key.

Analogy

A valet key. You would not hand a valet the master key to your car, house, and safe. A valet key starts the engine, opens the driver's door, and does nothing else; you can have it cancelled without changing any other lock. OAuth issues valet keys for online accounts. The key is called an access token; the "engine only" restriction is called a scope.

The four parties

OAuth conversations always involve four roles. Learning their names makes every OAuth diagram readable.

RoleWho it isIn "Sign in with Google" for the bakery app
Resource ownerThe user, who owns the data or identityDana
ClientThe application that wants access (a different sense of "client" than in Session 1)The bakery's web app
Authorization serverThe trusted service that authenticates the user and issues tokensGoogle's login and consent system
Resource serverThe service holding the data the token unlocksGoogle's profile or Calendar API

The authorization-code flow, step by step

Walk the class through it slowly; it is the most intricate diagram in the module and worth the time.

  1. Steps 1–3. The bakery's app does not show a password box. It sends Dana's browser to Google, telling Google which app is asking (a public client ID the bakery registered with Google beforehand) and what it wants (the scopes: here just email and name).
  2. Step 4. Dana logs in at Google, with Google's password box and Google's MFA. The bakery sees none of it. Google shows a consent screen listing exactly the scopes requested. Dana can refuse.
  3. Steps 5–6. Google sends the browser back to a pre-registered address at the bakery with a one-time authorization code. The code is deliberately useless on its own: it expires in a minute and can be redeemed only by the party holding the matching secret.
  4. Steps 7–8. The bakery's back end, in a direct server-to-server call the browser never sees, presents the code together with its client secret (a password that only the bakery's server and Google know). Google returns the access token, valid for about an hour, plus a longer-lived refresh token for obtaining new ones, plus an ID token describing who Dana is.
  5. Steps 9–10. The bakery uses the access token to ask Google for Dana's email and name, matches or creates her account, and issues its own ordinary session cookie. From here on, Session 4.3 applies.

Why the roundabout design? Because of what it protects against. Dana's password is never disclosed to the bakery. The token can do only what the scopes allow, so even a badly behaved app cannot read her email if it asked only for her name. Dana can see every app she has authorised in her Google account settings and revoke any of them with one click, instantly, without changing her password. And the access token expires quickly, so a stolen one has a short life. Compare each of those properties with the "type your Google password into our app" alternative and the value of the standard becomes obvious.

Login versus access: OpenID Connect

Strictly, OAuth is about authorization: granting an app access to resources. Using it for login (proving who the user is) was such a common desire that a thin standard was added on top: OpenID Connect (OIDC). It defines the ID token in step 8 and what it must contain. Every "Sign in with Google / Apple / Microsoft / GitHub" button is OIDC over OAuth. When a vendor says they support single sign-on (SSO), they mean a company's employees can log into the vendor's product with the company's central identity provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft Entra, Okta) using OIDC or its older enterprise cousin, SAML. For a business selling software to other businesses, supporting SSO is often a condition of the sale.

Business translation
  • Offering "Sign in with Google" raises sign-up conversion and removes your password-storage liability. Most new products should offer it alongside email and password.
  • When another app asks to "connect" to your Google, Slack, or bank account, read the scopes on the consent screen. That list is the entire extent of what it can do.
  • Your own product can be the resource server: letting partners "connect to your app" via OAuth is how platforms such as Shopify and Slack built their ecosystems.

4.6 Security basics every product owner should know 7 min

You do not need to be a security engineer, but a handful of ideas will let you ask the right questions and recognise the most common mistakes, several of which have already appeared in this module.

  • Encrypt in transit and at rest. HTTPS everywhere (in transit); encrypted disks and database volumes (at rest). Every cloud provider offers the latter as a checkbox. Turn it on.
  • Never trust the front end. Anything in the browser or the app can be read and altered by the user. Prices, discounts, permissions, and secrets belong on the server. This was the lesson of the three-tier diagram in Session 2.
  • Watch for injection. The most famous web vulnerability, SQL injection, happens when text a user types is pasted straight into a SQL query. If a login form builds SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ' + whatever was typed + ', then typing ' OR 1=1 -- makes the query true for every user. The fix (parameterised queries, where user input is passed to the database separately from the SQL) is automatic in every modern framework and ORM, which is one reason to use them. A cousin, cross-site scripting (XSS), does the same trick with HTML and JavaScript. The general rule: user input is data, never code.
  • Least privilege. Every person, program, and API key gets the minimum access it needs. The web server's database account should not be able to drop tables. An intern should not be an administrator. A leaked key that can only read is a nuisance; one that can do everything is a disaster.
  • Keep secrets out of code. Passwords, API keys, and client secrets go in environment configuration, never in source files and never in Git. Rotate any secret that has ever been exposed.
  • Keep software updated and take backups. Most breaches exploit known holes in unpatched software. Managed services (PaaS, managed databases) patch for you, which is a security argument for them, not only a convenience one. And test that backups actually restore; an untested backup is a hope, not a plan.

The industry maintains a list of the ten most common web application risks, published by an organisation called OWASP. You do not need to memorise it, but "have we reviewed against the OWASP Top Ten?" is a question that any engineer or AI coding assistant can act on, and asking it marks you as someone who knows what matters.

4.7 Beyond the browser: mobile, desktop, embedded 10 min

Everything so far has assumed the client is a browser. Most software you use is not a website, and yet almost all of it is built from the same parts. The distinction that matters is where the front end runs; the back end and the database are the same story.

Kind of softwareWhere the front end runsBuilt withDistributed howTrade-offs
Website / web appBrowserHTML, CSS, JavaScript (often with a framework such as React)Just a URL; nothing to install; updates instantlyLimited access to device hardware; needs a connection
Native mobile appPhone or tablet, installedSwift (iOS), Kotlin (Android)Apple App Store, Google Play; store review; 15–30% commission on in-app purchasesBest performance, full hardware access, offline use; two separate codebases to maintain
Cross-platform appPhone, installedReact Native, FlutterApp stores, same as nativeOne codebase for both platforms; slightly less polish and performance than native
Progressive web app (PWA)Browser, but installable to home screenWeb technologiesURL; no storeNo store commission or review; some features unavailable, especially on iPhone
Desktop applicationLaptop or PC, installedNative (C#, Swift, C++) or Electron (web technologies in a desktop wrapper: Slack, VS Code, Discord, Spotify)Download and installer, Mac App Store, Microsoft Store; must ship its own updatesFull power of the machine, works offline; installation friction, per-OS testing
Embedded softwareInside a device: thermostat, car, payment terminal, medical deviceC, C++, Rust; tiny processors, little memoryShipped inside the hardware; updated over the air, if at allHard to change after sale; reliability and security are paramount; the Internet of Things (IoT) connects them to the cloud
Command-line toolA terminal on a computerPython, Go, Rust, JavaScriptPackage managers (pip, npm, Homebrew)Text only; favoured by developers; Claude Code itself is one

This picture explains several things business people encounter:

  • Why "we need an app" is a smaller decision than it sounds. If the back end and API already exist, a mobile app is a new front end, not a new system. If they do not exist, the app project is secretly also a back-end project.
  • Why companies start with the web. A web app has no store review, no commission, instant updates, and one codebase. Native apps are added when the product needs the camera, notifications, offline use, or a home-screen presence.
  • Why the API is the product's most durable asset. Front ends are rewritten every few years as fashions and devices change; a well-designed API and its database outlive several generations of them.
  • Why embedded devices are the exception. A thermostat sold in 2026 must still work in 2036, may never be updated, and can physically harm someone if it fails. The engineering culture is correspondingly conservative, and the cost of a mistake is a recall rather than a redeploy.

4.8 Where AI fits 5 min

Since this course is about building products with AI, the last question is where a model such as Claude sits in everything above. The answer is reassuringly familiar: an AI model is a third-party API called from your back end. It is the Claude API box that has been sitting at the edge of the diagrams since Session 2.

Three practical consequences:

  • The key stays on the server. A model call from the browser would expose your API key to every visitor, who could run up your bill. All the reasoning of Section 4.4 applies.
  • Your data is the differentiator. The model is the same one your competitors can rent. What makes an AI feature yours is the context your back end adds from your database (this customer's history, your product catalogue, your policies) before calling the model. That pattern, fetching relevant data and putting it in the prompt, is what people mean by retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
  • AI calls have cost, latency, and failure modes. A model call takes seconds and costs money per word, so it is treated like any slow, paid third-party API: cached where possible, monitored, and given a fallback. When Claude Code builds an AI feature for you, these are the questions to ask it.

Step back and look at the whole module. A model such as Claude, the tool you are learning to build with, is itself served through exactly the architecture described here: a front end (the Claude app, or Claude Code in your terminal), load-balanced back ends behind an API, databases, caches, OAuth login, and an API key for programs. The next time you use it, you will know what is on the other end of the request.

Review questions

Session 4: Identity, security, and software beyond the browser

  1. Define authentication and authorization, and give an example where a system gets the first right and the second wrong.
  2. Why should a database store a hash of each password rather than the password itself? What does it mean if a company can email you your old password?
  3. HTTP is stateless, yet you stay logged in. Explain the role of the cookie and the session store.
  4. What does HTTP Basic Authentication send, in what form, and why is it acceptable only over HTTPS?
  5. Name the four roles in OAuth and identify each one when a scheduling app asks to read your Google Calendar.
  6. In the OAuth flow, why does Google send a one-time code back through the browser instead of the access token itself? And why does the user never type their Google password into the bakery's app?
  7. What is a scope in OAuth, and where does the user see it?
  8. What is SQL injection, and why does using a modern framework or ORM largely prevent it?
  9. Your company has a web app with a working API. The CEO wants "an iPhone app and an Android app." In architectural terms, how big is that project, and what alternative might you propose first?
  10. Where in a product's architecture does a call to an AI model such as Claude belong, and why must it not be made from the browser?

Answers are in Appendix B, Session 4.

Keywords Students Should Be Able to Define

Every highlighted keyword in the module, alphabetically, with a one-line definition and a link to the passage where it is introduced. Suggested use: hand out as a study sheet, or quiz students on a random sample at the start of each session.

JSONJavaScript Object Notation. The standard text format for exchanging data between programs over the web: values in curly braces with 'name': value pairs and square brackets for lists. Human-readable and understood by every programming language.2.2 APIs and JSON: how programs talk to programs
L
LatencyThe delay between a request being sent and the response arriving, usually measured in milliseconds. Users notice anything over about 100 ms; a page taking more than 3 seconds loses a large fraction of visitors.3.2 Step 1: everything on one server
load balancerA component that receives all incoming requests and distributes them across a pool of identical servers, so that no one server is overloaded and a failed server is skipped automatically. The public address of a scaled website points at its load balancer.3.4 Step 3: many web servers behind a load balancer
localhostThe name a computer uses for itself. Opening http://localhost:5000 in a browser connects to a server program running on your own machine, which is how developers test before deploying.2.2 APIs and JSON: how programs talk to programs
M
managed databaseA database run for you by a cloud provider (Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL, Supabase, Neon, PlanetScale): they handle installation, backups, security patches, and failover; you get a connection address and a monthly bill.3.4 Step 3: many web servers behind a load balancer
methodThe verb at the start of an HTTP request that says what kind of action is wanted. GET reads, POST creates or submits, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes.2.2 APIs and JSON: how programs talk to programs
MonitoringContinuously collecting measurements and log messages from a running system (errors, response times, traffic, server health) and alerting people when something goes wrong, so problems are found before customers report them.3.7 Shipping code safely
Multi-factor authenticationMulti-Factor Authentication: requiring two or more independent proofs of identity, typically something you know (a password) plus something you have (a code from your phone, a hardware key) or something you are (a fingerprint). Blocks most account takeovers even when the password is stolen.4.3 Staying logged in: cookies, sessions, and tokens
N
Native mobile appA mobile or desktop application written in the platform's own language and tools (Swift for iPhone, Kotlin for Android) and installed on the device. Fastest and most capable on that platform, but a separate codebase per platform.4.7 Beyond the browser: mobile, desktop, embedded
NoSQLA family of databases that do not use the table-and-SQL model. Document databases (MongoDB) store JSON-like records with flexible shapes; key-value stores (Redis) hold simple lookups very fast. Chosen for flexibility or speed at very large scale.2.6 Putting it together: the three-tier architecture
O
OAuth 2.0OAuth 2.0: the standard protocol that lets a user grant one application limited access to their account at another service (or prove their identity to it) without ever sharing their password. The user is sent to the trusted service to approve specific permissions, and the application receives a scoped, revocable access token instead of the password. Behind every 'Sign in with Google' button.4.5 OAuth: how "Sign in with Google" works
object storageA cloud service for storing files of any size (images, documents, video, backups) at very low cost and reachable from anywhere by URL. Amazon S3 is the original; every cloud has an equivalent. The standard home for user uploads.3.5 Step 4: caches, CDNs, and storage
OpenID ConnectOpenID Connect: a layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that standardises using it for login. The authorization server returns an ID token stating who the user is, which is what 'Sign in with Google/Apple/Microsoft' actually uses.4.6 Security basics every product owner should know
operating systemThe base software that manages a computer's hardware and runs programs: Linux on almost all servers, Windows and macOS on desktops, iOS and Android on phones.3.2 Step 1: everything on one server
ORMObject-Relational Mapper: a library that lets a program work with database rows as ordinary objects in its own language (Python, JavaScript) and writes the SQL behind the scenes. SQLAlchemy, Django ORM, and Prisma are examples.2.6 Putting it together: the three-tier architecture
P
PaaSPlatform as a Service: you hand the provider your code and they run it, handling servers, operating systems, scaling, HTTPS, and often the database. Less control, far less work. Heroku, Render, Railway, Vercel, Fly.io.3.6 The cloud menu: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, serverless
pathThe part of a URL after the domain, such as /menu.html or /products/42, that identifies which page, file, or resource on the server is being requested.1.5 How the internet delivers a page
portA numbered 'door' on a computer that a server program listens on, so that one machine can run several services. Web traffic uses port 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS); developers often run test servers on ports like 3000, 5000, or 8000.2.2 APIs and JSON: how programs talk to programs
primary keyA column whose value uniquely identifies each row in a table, such as customer_id. No two rows share one, and it never changes, so it can be used to refer to that row from anywhere.2.3 Why every product needs a database
private networkA network inside a data center or cloud account that is not reachable from the public internet. Databases and internal services are placed on it so that only your own servers can connect to them.3.4 Step 3: many web servers behind a load balancer
Progressive web appProgressive Web App: a website built so that it can be installed to the home screen, work offline, and send notifications, blurring the line between website and app. Distributed by URL, not through an app store.4.7 Beyond the browser: mobile, desktop, embedded
protocolAn agreed set of rules for how two computers exchange messages, so that programs written by different people can still understand each other. HTTP, HTTPS, and DNS are all protocols.1.5 How the internet delivers a page
Q
queryA question or instruction sent to a database, written in SQL. 'Running a query' means asking the database for data or telling it to change data.2.4 SQL by example
query stringThe optional part of a URL after a question mark, made of name=value pairs such as ?lang=en&page=2, used to pass extra details to the server.1.5 How the internet delivers a page
R
read replicaA live copy of the database that is continuously kept up to date from the primary. Read replicas answer read-only queries to take load off the primary; a standby replica takes over if the primary fails.3.5 Step 4: caches, CDNs, and storage
relational modelThe way of organising data into tables of rows and columns, where each table describes one kind of thing (customers, orders) and tables are linked to each other by shared identifying values (keys). Managed by relational databases and queried with SQL.2.3 Why every product needs a database
renderingThe process by which a browser turns HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into the visible page on screen.1.5 How the internet delivers a page
requestThe message a client sends to a server asking for something. An HTTP request names a method (GET, POST, and so on), a path, and headers with extra details, and may carry a body of data.1.5 How the internet delivers a page
responseThe message a server sends back to a client after a request. An HTTP response carries a status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found), headers, and usually a body such as an HTML page or JSON data.1.5 How the internet delivers a page
RESTA widely used style for designing web APIs in which each URL names a resource (a product, an order) and the HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) says what to do with it. 'A REST API' is the most common kind of API a business will build or consume.2.2 APIs and JSON: how programs talk to programs
retrieval-augmented generationRetrieval-Augmented Generation: having the back end look up relevant information (from a database, documents, or search) and include it in the prompt, so the AI model answers using your data rather than only what it learned in training.4.8 Where AI fits
rolesA named bundle of permissions assigned to users, such as customer, staff, or administrator, so that access rules are written once per role instead of once per person. Role-based access control (RBAC) is the common name for this approach.4.2 Passwords done right
routeA rule in a back-end program that says which function should run when a request arrives for a particular path, such as /hours or /orders/42. Routing is the act of matching incoming paths to code.2.1 Inside the back end: a Python web server
S
SaaSSoftware as a Service: finished software you use through a browser or app and pay for by subscription, with nothing to install or run. Gmail, Salesforce, Shopify, Slack, Notion.3.6 The cloud menu: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, serverless
schemaThe blueprint of a database: which tables exist, what columns each has, what type of data each column holds, and how tables link to one another through keys.2.4 SQL by example
scopesIn OAuth, a named permission the application asks for, such as 'read email address' or 'read calendar events'. The user sees the scopes on the consent screen and the issued token can do nothing beyond them.4.5 OAuth: how "Sign in with Google" works
serverA computer, or a program on a computer, that waits for requests from clients and answers them. Servers are ordinary computers, usually in a data center, running around the clock.1.2 Clients, servers, and programs
ServerlessA cloud model in which you upload individual functions and the provider runs each one only when a request arrives, charging per execution. No servers to manage or pay for while idle; scales from zero to millions automatically. AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Functions.3.7 Shipping code safely
session IDThe server's record that a particular user has logged in, identified by a long random session ID that is stored in the user's cookie. On each request the server looks up the ID to learn who is asking. Sessions expire after a period or on logout.4.3 Staying logged in: cookies, sessions, and tokens
single point of failureAny single component whose failure takes the whole system down. Removing single points of failure by adding duplicates is the main way to increase uptime.3.3 Step 2: give the database its own machine
single sign-onSingle Sign-On: logging in once with a central identity provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft Entra, Okta) and being recognised by many applications without separate passwords. Built on OpenID Connect or the older SAML standard; a standard requirement for selling software to companies.4.6 Security basics every product owner should know
SQLStructured Query Language, the standard language for asking questions of and making changes to a relational database. Statements read almost like English: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, JOIN.2.4 SQL by example
SQL injectionAn attack in which text a user types (in a form or URL) is pasted into a SQL query and ends up being run as part of the query, letting the attacker read or destroy data. Prevented by parameterised queries, which every modern framework and ORM uses by default.4.7 Beyond the browser: mobile, desktop, embedded
statelessA server that keeps no memory of previous requests between one request and the next. Any copy can handle any request because everything that must be remembered (who is logged in, what is in the cart) is stored in a shared database or cache, not on the server itself.3.5 Step 4: caches, CDNs, and storage
static websiteA website made of fixed files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images) that are delivered to every visitor exactly as stored. Nothing is computed per visitor and no data is saved on the server.1.5 How the internet delivers a page
status codeThe three-digit number in an HTTP response that says how the request went. 200 means success, 301 means moved, 404 means not found, 500 means the server hit an error.1.5 How the internet delivers a page
T
tablesIn a relational database, a grid holding all records of one kind of thing. Each row is one record (one customer) and each column is one attribute (name, email).2.3 Why every product needs a database
tagsA label in angle brackets, such as <h1> or <p>, that HTML uses to mark what a piece of content is. Most tags come in pairs: an opening tag and a closing tag with a slash.1.3 A web page is three languages
templatesAn HTML file with placeholders (such as {{ customer_name }}) that the back end fills in with real data before sending the page. Templates keep page design separate from program logic.2.2 APIs and JSON: how programs talk to programs
third-party APIAn API offered by another company that your product calls to get a capability without building it: payments (Stripe), maps (Google), text messages (Twilio), AI (Claude API). Usually paid per use.2.3 Why every product needs a database
three-tier architectureThe classic structure of a web application in three layers: the presentation tier (front end in the browser or app), the application or logic tier (back-end program), and the data tier (database). Each tier can be built, scaled, and replaced separately.2.6 Putting it together: the three-tier architecture
tokenA string handed to a client after it authenticates, which the client then attaches to each request as proof of identity, instead of sending a password every time. Session IDs, API keys, JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), and OAuth access tokens are all kinds of tokens.4.4 HTTP Basic Authentication and API keys
transactionA group of database changes that either all succeed or all fail together, so the data is never left half-updated. Moving money between two accounts is the classic example.2.3 Why every product needs a database
U
UptimeThe fraction of time a service is working and reachable, usually quoted as a percentage. 99.9% uptime ('three nines') allows about 9 hours of downtime a year; 99.99% allows about 53 minutes.3.2 Step 1: everything on one server
URLUniform Resource Locator, the full address of something on the web. It names the protocol (https), the domain (which server), and the path (which page or file on that server).1.5 How the internet delivers a page
V
Version controlA system that records every change to a project's code, who made it, and why, so that changes can be reviewed, combined, and undone. Git is the universal tool; GitHub and GitLab host Git repositories online for teams.3.7 Shipping code safely
Vertical scalingAdding capacity by making one machine bigger: more processor cores, more memory, faster disks. Simple, but has a hard ceiling and the machine remains a single point of failure.3.4 Step 3: many web servers behind a load balancer
virtual private serversVirtual Private Server: a rented slice of a physical server in a data center that behaves like your own dedicated computer, with its own operating system, IP address, and disk. The cheapest way to run a back end on the internet; typically 5 to 50 dollars a month.3.2 Step 1: everything on one server
W
web browserA program such as Chrome, Safari, Firefox, or Edge that requests web pages from servers and turns the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript it receives into what you see on screen.1.3 A web page is three languages
web serverA program that listens for web requests and sends back web pages and files. Popular examples are Nginx and Apache. The word also refers to the computer running that program.1.2 Clients, servers, and programs
Appendix B

Review Questions and Answers

The review questions from the end of each session, repeated here with model answers. Answers are written at the level of detail expected from a student; a shorter answer that captures the same ideas is fine.

Session 1: From a file to a page on the internet

  1. In the client–server model, which side starts every conversation, and why does that matter for how servers are designed?The client always starts. The server only waits and answers. This means a server must be always on and reachable, and it never needs to "find" its users; it just has to handle whatever arrives. It also means a server cannot push you information you did not ask for without tricks such as the browser repeatedly asking.
  2. A web page is written in up to three languages. Name each one and state in one phrase what it is responsible for.HTML describes the content and structure (headings, paragraphs, images, links). CSS controls appearance (colors, fonts, spacing, layout). JavaScript controls behaviour and interactivity (reacting to clicks, changing the page, fetching data).
  3. Why can you open a static website from a folder on your desktop with no internet connection, but your friend across town cannot see it?A static site is just files, and a browser can read files straight off the local disk (the address begins with file:///). Your friend's browser cannot reach files on your computer because your machine is not a publicly addressable, always-on server. To share it, the files must be placed on a hosted server with a domain name pointing to it.
  4. Break the URL https://shop.example.com/products/42?color=blue into its parts and say what each part tells the browser.https is the protocol (talk securely using HTTP). shop.example.com is the domain name, identifying which server to contact (shop is a subdomain of example.com). /products/42 is the path, identifying which resource on that server (product number 42). ?color=blue is the query string, an extra detail passed as a name=value pair.
  5. What does DNS do, and what everyday object is it usually compared to?DNS translates a human-readable domain name into the numeric IP address of the server hosting it. It is compared to a phone book or contacts list: you look up a name and get a number you can actually dial.
  6. A customer reports seeing "500 Internal Server Error" while another reports "404 Not Found." Which one suggests a bug in your own code, and which suggests a bad link or typo?500 means the server's own program failed while handling the request, so it points to a bug or outage on your side. 404 means the server is fine but no such page exists at that path, which usually indicates a broken link, a deleted page, or a typo in the address.
  7. Give two things a purely static website cannot do, and explain in one sentence what has to be added to do them.Any two of: remember information a visitor submits, personalise pages per visitor, keep a secret such as a payment key, or perform work such as sending emails or charging cards. To do them you add a back end: a program on the server that runs per request, applies logic, and reads and writes stored data.
  8. Your Python course teaches you to write programs. In a web application, where would that Python code run, and why not in the visitor's browser?Python runs on the server as back-end code (or on your own computer as a script). It does not run in the browser because browsers only execute JavaScript; that is the one language every browser was built to understand.

Back to the Session 1 review box

Session 2: Dynamic websites, APIs, and databases

  1. In the Flask example, what does a route do, and what is the difference between the / route and the /hours route from the visitor's point of view?A route connects a URL path to a function in the back end; when a request for that path arrives, the function runs and its return value becomes the response. The / route returns the same HTML every time, so it behaves like a static page. The /hours route checks the current time and returns different HTML depending on the answer, which is what makes it dynamic.
  2. Explain what an API is using the restaurant analogy, then give a real example of a third-party API a small business might call and why.An API is like a restaurant menu: a fixed list of what you may ask for and what you will receive, which lets outsiders use the kitchen without seeing inside it. Example: calling Stripe's API to charge a credit card, because building payment processing yourself is expensive, risky, and heavily regulated. Other valid answers: Twilio for text messages, Google Maps for addresses, the Claude API for text generation.
  3. What is JSON, and why did it become the standard format for APIs?JSON is a text format for data: curly braces hold named values, square brackets hold lists, text is quoted, numbers and true/false stand alone. It became the standard because it is human-readable, compact, maps directly onto the data structures of nearly every programming language (a Python dictionary, for instance), and is natively understood by JavaScript in the browser.
  4. Match each HTTP method to a CRUD operation and give a bakery example for each.POST = Create (place an order: POST /api/orders). GET = Read (list products: GET /api/products). PUT or PATCH = Update (mark an order ready: PATCH /api/orders/88). DELETE = Delete (cancel an order: DELETE /api/orders/88).
  5. Give three reasons a business stores its data in a database rather than in ordinary files.Any three of: many users and programs can write at the same time without corrupting the data; searches over millions of records are fast thanks to indexes; transactions guarantee changes are all-or-nothing so data is never left half-saved; complex questions (reports) can be asked in one line of SQL; constraints such as "every order must have a customer" are enforced automatically.
  6. In the bakery schema, why does the orders table store a customer_id instead of the customer's name and email? Which term describes that column?Storing the ID avoids copying the same customer details into every order. If Dana changes her email, it is updated once in the customers table and every order automatically reflects it; copies would drift out of sync. A column that holds another table's primary key is a foreign key.
  7. In plain English, what does this query return?
    SELECT customers.name, COUNT(*) FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id GROUP BY customers.name;    For each customer who has placed at least one order, it returns the customer's name and the number of orders they have placed. The JOIN attaches the customer's name to each order via the customer_id key, and GROUP BY with COUNT tallies the orders per name.
  8. What is dangerous about the statement DELETE FROM orders; and what single addition would make it safe?It has no WHERE clause, so it deletes every row in the orders table, not just one. Adding a WHERE condition such as WHERE order_id = 89 restricts it to the intended row. This is also why production databases are backed up and why write permissions are restricted.
  9. Name the three tiers of the three-tier architecture and state which tier enforces the rule "customers get 10% off orders over $50" and why it must be there.Presentation tier (front end in the browser or app), application tier (back-end program), and data tier (database). The discount rule belongs in the application tier, on the server. Anything in the browser can be altered by the user, so a rule enforced only in the front end could be bypassed to get a discount on any order.

Back to the Session 2 review box

Session 3: Hosting, scaling, and the cloud

  1. What does "deploy" mean, and why do teams put a staging environment between development and production?To deploy is to put a version of the software onto servers where real users can reach it. Staging is a private replica of production where the team checks a release with realistic data and settings before customers see it, catching the differences between "works on my machine" and the live system.
  2. Describe the Step 1 single-server deployment and name its most serious weakness.One rented machine (a VPS running Linux) hosts the web server program, the back-end application, and the database together. Its most serious weakness is that it is a single point of failure: a disk failure, power loss, or a botched update takes down the website and the data at the same time. It also suffers from resource contention and has a hard capacity ceiling.
  3. Give two reasons for moving the database onto its own server, and explain what "private network" means in that design.Reasons (any two): each machine can be sized for its own job (databases want memory and fast disks); security improves because the database is no longer on the machine exposed to the internet; the web server can be rebuilt without touching data; it enables running several web servers that share one database. A private network is one with no route from the public internet: only the company's own servers can connect to the database, enforced by firewall rules.
  4. Explain the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling. Which one does modern web architecture rely on, and why?Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger (more processor, memory). Horizontal scaling adds more identical machines and spreads work across them. Modern architecture relies on horizontal scaling because it has no hard ceiling, tolerates the failure of any single machine, and lets capacity grow and shrink with demand, whereas a single big machine remains a single point of failure and eventually cannot be made bigger.
  5. What does a load balancer do, and what is a health check?A load balancer holds the public address, receives every incoming request, and distributes requests across the pool of web servers so none is overloaded. A health check is a small request it sends to each server every few seconds; a server that fails to respond correctly is removed from rotation until it recovers, so customers never reach a broken server.
  6. Why must web servers be stateless in a load-balanced setup? Where does the "state" go instead?Because the load balancer may send a user's consecutive requests to different servers, any server that remembered something locally (such as "this person is logged in") would leave the others ignorant of it, and the site would appear broken. Servers therefore keep nothing between requests; who is logged in, cart contents, and all other shared facts live in a shared store every server can reach, such as the database or a Redis session store.
  7. A customer in Tokyo complains that images load slowly from your site hosted in Virginia. Which component fixes this and how?A content delivery network (CDN). It keeps copies of static files (images, CSS, JavaScript, video) on servers in cities around the world, so the Tokyo customer receives the image from a nearby server in a few milliseconds instead of waiting for it to cross the Pacific. It also removes that traffic from your own servers.
  8. What is a cache, and what is the one hard problem every cache has?A cache is a fast temporary copy of data that was expensive to compute or fetch, kept so the next request for it is answered instantly (for example a product list stored in memory instead of re-running the SQL query). The hard problem is staleness: the copy can be out of date, so someone must decide how long it may live and when it must be refreshed or discarded.
  9. Place each of these on the IaaS / PaaS / SaaS / serverless menu: renting a virtual machine on AWS EC2; using Shopify to run a store; connecting a GitHub repo to Render so it runs your code; running a small function on AWS Lambda when a file is uploaded.EC2 virtual machine = IaaS (you manage everything on it). Shopify = SaaS (finished software by subscription). Render running your code = PaaS (you provide code, they run the servers). Lambda function on upload = serverless (a single function run and billed per event).
  10. You are deploying a prototype built with Claude Code for a business school project. Which layer of the cloud menu is the sensible choice and why?PaaS (Render, Railway, Vercel, Fly.io) with a managed database (Supabase, Neon). It provides HTTPS, deployment from GitHub, load balancing, and horizontal scaling with no servers to administer, for little or no money, which matches a small team with no operations expertise. IaaS adds work without benefit at this scale.

Back to the Session 3 review box

Session 4: Identity, security, and software beyond the browser

  1. Define authentication and authorization, and give an example where a system gets the first right and the second wrong.Authentication verifies who a user is (password, code, fingerprint, Google login). Authorization decides what that identified user may do. Example of getting only the first right: a site that checks you are logged in but lets you view any order by changing the number in the URL, so any customer can read any other customer's order.
  2. Why should a database store a hash of each password rather than the password itself? What does it mean if a company can email you your old password?A hash is a one-way scramble that cannot be reversed to recover the password, so if the database is stolen the attackers cannot read users' passwords (which people reuse elsewhere). Login works by hashing what the user types and comparing. If a company can send you your old password, it is storing passwords in readable form, which is a serious security failure.
  3. HTTP is stateless, yet you stay logged in. Explain the role of the cookie and the session store.On login the server creates a session record ("ID a8f3… = Dana, expires in 14 days") in a shared session store and tells the browser to save the ID in a cookie. The browser automatically sends the cookie with every later request; the server looks up the ID and knows who is asking. Any web server in the pool can do this lookup, which is what allows servers to be stateless.
  4. What does HTTP Basic Authentication send, in what form, and why is it acceptable only over HTTPS?It sends the username and password on every request in an Authorization header, encoded in Base64 (for example Base64 of "dana:correct-horse"). Base64 is encoding, not encryption, and is instantly reversible, so over plain HTTP the password would be readable by anyone on the network. HTTPS encrypts the whole exchange, which is the only thing keeping the credentials private.
  5. Name the four roles in OAuth and identify each one when a scheduling app asks to read your Google Calendar.Resource owner: you, the user who owns the calendar. Client: the scheduling app requesting access. Authorization server: Google's login and consent system, which authenticates you and issues the token. Resource server: the Google Calendar API that holds the data the token unlocks.
  6. In the OAuth flow, why does Google send a one-time code back through the browser instead of the access token itself? And why does the user never type their Google password into the bakery's app?The code is useless on its own: it expires quickly and can only be exchanged for a token by presenting the client secret, which lives on the bakery's server. Exchanging it in a server-to-server call means the token never passes through the browser where it could be intercepted or leaked. The user types their password only at Google so the bakery never possesses it; the bakery receives a scoped, expiring, revocable token instead, which limits damage if the app is careless or compromised.
  7. What is a scope in OAuth, and where does the user see it?A scope is a named, limited permission the application requests, such as "read your email address" or "read calendar events." The user sees the requested scopes on the consent screen at the authorization server (Google) before approving, and the issued token can do nothing beyond them.
  8. What is SQL injection, and why does using a modern framework or ORM largely prevent it?SQL injection occurs when text a user types is pasted directly into a SQL statement so that it runs as part of the query; typing ' OR 1=1 -- into a login form could make the query match every user. Modern frameworks and ORMs use parameterised queries, which send user input to the database separately from the SQL text so it is always treated as data, never as code.
  9. Your company has a web app with a working API. The CEO wants "an iPhone app and an Android app." In architectural terms, how big is that project, and what alternative might you propose first?Because the back end and API already exist, the apps are new front ends rather than a new system: the mobile apps call the same API and use the same data and login. It is still real work (two native codebases or one cross-platform codebase, app store review, updates). A cheaper first step is a progressive web app, which is installable to the home screen from the existing web app with no store involvement, unless the product needs native-only features such as rich offline use or certain hardware access.
  10. Where in a product's architecture does a call to an AI model such as Claude belong, and why must it not be made from the browser?In the back end (application tier), as a call to a third-party API, after the back end has checked who is asking and gathered relevant data from the database to include in the prompt. It must not be made from the browser because the API key would then be visible to every visitor, who could use it to run up the company's bill, and because the business rules and private data added to the prompt must stay on the server.

Back to the Session 4 review box

Appendix C

Suggested Follow-Up Activities

  • Architecture sketch. In pairs, students pick a familiar product (a food-delivery app, a ticketing site, a fitness tracker with a phone app and a wearable) and draw its architecture using only the boxes from this module: front ends, load balancer, web servers, database, cache, CDN, object storage, third-party APIs, AI model. Present and critique.
  • Read a real API. Open the public documentation for Stripe, Shopify, or the Claude API. Identify three endpoints, their HTTP methods, and the JSON they return. Find where authentication is described and name the mechanism (API key, OAuth, or both).
  • Consent-screen audit. Students review the third-party apps connected to their own Google or Microsoft account, list the scopes each was granted, and revoke any they no longer use. Discuss what each scope allowed.
  • Deploy something. With Claude Code, build the bakery's Flask app with an SQLite database, then deploy it to a free PaaS tier. Students document which cloud-menu layer they used, what the platform handled for them, and what the monthly cost would be at 10× traffic.
  • Vendor conversation role-play. One student plays a founder, another an agency proposing a build. The founder must ask at least five questions from this module (where does the database live, can we run two copies, who holds the API keys, do we support Sign in with Google, what is the uptime target) and judge the answers.
